label: religious concepts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religious concepts as: Ideas and notions that are fundamentally religious.

label: philosophical concepts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines philosophical concepts as: Concepts related to knowledge, learning, and scholarship.

label: Styles and Periods Facet
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Styles and Periods Facet as: Includes the names of art and architecture styles, historical periods, art movements, cultures, and ethnicities. Names of people and sites are included if they designate distinct styles or periods. Examples: Yoruba, Louis XIV, Aztec, German, Neolithic.

label: book history
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines book history as: Research into the evolution of the book and its variants (pamphlets, newspapers, broadsheets) in all aspects of its production, dissemination and consumption in relation to literary, political, economical, social and religious history. The history of the book includes subjects such as the production of manuscripts in medieval scriptoria, authorship, printing techniques, economic aspects of printing and publishing, design, printshops and publishing houses, trade, ownership and reading culture, typography, typesetting and printing techniques, and book collecting and connoisseurship. Use " literary history" Use “literary history” for the study of literary trends and movements.

label: literary studies
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines literary studies as: Discipline dealing with the written and oral verbal works of a nation, region, period, or language, of a particular group or individual, of a particular form or genre, on a particular subject, or for a particular audience. For written works on a particular subject, use "literature (documents)." For the written works of a particular individual or group of individuals, use "writings (documents)." For the genre of liturature rather than the discipline that studies it, use "literature (genre)." Use "book history" for the study of the trade, production, and consumption of books as physical objects.

label: museology
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines museology as: The theory and practice of the organization, administration, functions, and technical processes of museums, including documentation and collections management, as well as their history, philosophy, and purposes.

label: paper history
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines paper history as: Study of the origin and evolution of paper as a product and material: paper production, paper trade, the management of papermills and paper factories, raw materials, and the cultural importance of paper as an information carrier.

label: auspicia
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines auspicia as: In ancient Roman religion, the signs of the gods that were inscribed in nature and meant to be deciphered. Auspicia were seen as affirmative or negative answers to proposed courses of action. Auspicia often came from the sky as thunder, lightning, and different kinds of birds although there were other kinds as well. Public auspicia were taken by magistrates or augurs in the sacred space of the templum.

label: biblical
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines biblical as: Of, relating to, or contained in the Bible, which contains the sacred scriptures of Judaism or Christianity.

label: blasphemy
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines blasphemy as: An irreverent or impious act, attitude, or utterance regarding something considered inviolable or sacrosanct, particularly something concerning God.

label: cultism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines cultism as: Having to do with the formation or following of a cult, which is a religious group having beliefs that differ significantly from dominant or orthodox religions or society.

label: divine judgment
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines divine judgment as: Actions and status of a dvinity's retributive justice by which the destiny of people or other creatures is decided, typically according to their merits and demerits.

label: doctrinal concepts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines doctrinal concepts as: Religious concepts related to doctrine.

label: Dreaming, the
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Dreaming, the as: A fundamental concept of Australian aboriginal religion that refers to a mythological period of time before living memory when the world was shaped and humanized by the actions of mythic ancestral beings. Some of these beings were in human or animal (totemic) form while others changed their form. They were responsible for creating the different types of plants and animals, including humans, as well as for establishing local social order and laws to live by. In aboriginal belief, these ancestors are spiritually as much alive today as they ever were. As a belief system, the Dreaming includes totemism: man is regarded as part of nature, not fundamentally different from his mythic ancestors or from animals, all of which share a common life force. This connection is often made visible through the use of totem figures.

label: heresy
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines heresy as: Theological or religious opinion or doctrine maintained in opposition to the official or orthodox doctrine of a given church, creed, or religious system.

label: monasticism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines monasticism as: A form of religious life that emphasizes the perfection of the individual through immersion in a consecrated community or, more rarely, through a solitary and ascetic existence. Monasticism is found in both Buddhism and Christianity, particularly in the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches. Although it began as a lay movement in Christianity, clergy soon came to dominate and it began to involve voluntary poverty and a life devoted to worship. The rule of Benedict was the most important early monastic legislation and it became the standard of Western Christian monasticism. The mendicant orders, which combined monastic life with missionary work and preaching, were created in the 13th century. Scholarship was emphasized in some medieval monastic systems, which led to important religious research and manuscripts.

label: private devotion
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines private devotion as: The psychological process of experiencing devotional feelings in a private sphere, whether or not encouraged by the church authorities, often with the aid of texts, figurines or images.

label: rabbinical
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines rabbinical as: Of, relating to, or characteristic of the teachings of rabbis that constitute the Talmud.

label: religious ideologies
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religious ideologies as: Organized bodies of ideas and attitudes having to do with religion, which is broadly defined as belief systems that encompass various personal and institutional relationships between human beings and what they regard as holy, sacred, or divine, usually but not always a deity, or a spiritual or occult force.

label: worship
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines worship as: The reverent love and allegiance accorded a deity, idol, or sacred object, often expressed through ceremonies, prayers, or other religious rituals.

label: aesthetic concepts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines aesthetic concepts as: Concepts related to perception of what is ideal or beautiful.

label: betrayal
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines betrayal as: Violation of trust or confidence or an abandonment of something committed to one's charge, such as a revelation or divulging of something which it is desirable to keep secret or a treacherous giving up to an enemy.

label: cosmos
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines cosmos as: An ordered and harmonious system that comprises the world or universe.

label: evil
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines evil as: The state of a person or situation of being morally depraved, bad, wicked, or vicious. The antithesis of "good."

label: fate
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines fate as: The principle, power, or agency by which, according to certain philosophical and popular systems of belief, all events, or some events in particular, are unalterably predetermined from eternity.

label: fortitude
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines fortitude as: Moral strength or courage, unyielding courage, endurance of pain or adversity.

label: fortune
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines fortune as: Chance or luck, when regarded as a cause of events and changes in human affairs.

label: hope
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines hope as: The expectation of something desired.

label: hózhó
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines hózhó as: Philosophical concept central to Navajo aesthetics and culture. Advocates for individuals to be balanced and in harmony with other spiritual and material aspects of Navajo life (landscape, community, etc.) In Navajo material culture and art, beauty is achieved through this balance. This concept can be seen expressed in textiles and pottery through their balanced compositions and in sandpainting in its illustrations of interconnected, harmonious relationships between people, animals, spirits, and the land. Also is applied to contemporary art made by Navajo artists.

label: ideology
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ideology as: Any organized body of ideas and attitudes, especially about the structure and working of human society, that comprehends a program of practical political and social action and is more or less institutionalized or shared with others. Originally used for a branch of knowledge dealing with the history and nature of ideas.

label: ignorance
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ignorance as: The fact or condition of lacking knowledge or awareness, either generally or about a particular thing.

label: immortality
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines immortality as: In philosophical and religious traditions, the concept of or belief in the continued existence of a material thing into infinity, or of the existance of an immaterial soul or mind beyond the physical death of the body.

label: inventiveness
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines inventiveness as: The quality, faculty, or aptitude for creating unique solutions to problems, or of inventng new things, language, art, etc.

label: metaphysical concepts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines metaphysical concepts as: Philosophical concepts that deal with the nature of reality.

label: morality
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines morality as: Ethical wisdom, knowledge, or qualities, as evidenced in behavior conforming to moral law or accepted moral standards, particularly in relation to sexual matters or personal qualities judged to be good.

label: prudence
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines prudence as: Concept concerning the ability to recognize and follow the most suitable or sensible course of action, utilizing good sense, discretion, circumspection, caution.

label: survival
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines survival as: The state or fact of the continuance of anything after the end of other like things within the same context, as after some event. The persistence of a living thing, custom, or observance, after the circumstances or conditions in which it originated or which gave significance to it have ceased.

label: truth
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines truth as: A property of beliefs, propositions, and linguistic statements, being that they conform with fact or agree with reality.

label: vengeance
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines vengeance as: The act or condition of inflicting retributive injury or punishment in retaliation for an injury or offense.

label: wisdom
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines wisdom as: Accumulated learning and soundness of judgment in the choice of means and ends.

label: world
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines world as: The state or realm of existence, particularly of the physical.

label: theater arts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines theater arts as: Broad discipline concerning drama, dance, critical studies, and theater design/technology; a professionally-oriented study of theater, that involves training, practice, and study in the processes of doing theater.

label: electronic music
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines electronic music as: Music in which sound is generated, transferred, triggered, or amplified by electronic devices. The creation of electronic music may involve the use of magnetic tape or digital technology and whose reproduction involves the use of loudspeakers. For works created with only natural sound sources recorded and manipulated via discs or magnetic tape use "musique concrète." For music created entirely through the use of a computer, in which the sound is initiated purely through digital means, use "computer music."

label: jazz
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines jazz as: Music, often improvisational, originally developed around the turn of the 20th century by African Americans from elements of blues and ragtime, with syncopated rhythms and a European harmonic structure. Jazz consistently evolved throughout the 20th century with numerous phases, from a New Orleans style or swing, to "free jazz," for example, which emerged in the late 1950s. Therefore, jazz itself has no precise definition, however it has rarely been a completely composed music.

label: musical theater
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines musical theater as: Genre of theatrical performance that combines songs, spoken dialogue, acting, and dance.

label: rhythm and blues
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines rhythm and blues as: Any of various kinds of popular music typically having a strong rhythm and featuring a horn section. Originally and principally associated with African-American performers, particularly a style prominent during the late 1940s and 1950s derived from or influenced by the blues and jazz.

label: serial music
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines serial music as: A structural principle for musical composition used since the early 20th century in which a series or set of elements are used repeatedly.

label: myths
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines myths as: Individual stories derived from a mythology; distinguished from historical accounts in that they are considered by current scholars to lack a determinable basis of fact or natural explanation; typically concerning a being, hero, deity, or event and explains some practice, rite, or phenomenon of nature.

label: arts-related disciplines
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines arts-related disciplines as: Branches of learning devoted to the arts.

label: linguistics
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines linguistics as: Scientific study of language as a system, covering the structure, sounds, and meaning, as well as the history of the relations of languages to each other and the cultural place of language in human behavior.

label: linguistics-related disciplines
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines linguistics-related disciplines as: Branches of learning and professions related to linguistics.

label: comparative literature
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines comparative literature as: The study of similar literary works from two or more nations, periods, or languages in relation to each other, or the study of any literary phenomenon from the perspective of at least two literatures.

label: literary criticism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines literary criticism as: The discipline of describing, interpreting, and evaluating literary works, including the exposition of principles, methods, and theories for the analysis of such works.

label: literary history
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines literary history as: Study of literary trends and movements over time, as well as the development of various branches or genres of literature.

label: poetics
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines poetics as: The theory, art, or study of the nature and function of poetry and with identifying and describing its types, forms, and techniques.

label: museography
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines museography as: Refers to museum methods of classification, description and display of objects; the practical application of the body of theory known as museology.

label: museum administration
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines museum administration as: The study and practice of the administration of museums.

label: aesthetics
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines aesthetics as: Appreciation or criticism of the beautiful. The term refers to a branch of Western philosophy concerned primarily with the fine arts, although it may also be used in the context of the appreciation of natural beauty. Usage of the term dates from the 18th century, although historical discussions regarding issues now called "aesthetics" date from Antiquity.

label: axiology
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines axiology as: Study of values, primarily of intrinsic values (as those in ethics, aesthetics, and religion), but also of instrumental values (as those in economics), particularly with reference to the manner in which they can be known or experienced, their nature and kinds, and their ontological status.

label: epistemology
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines epistemology as: Branch of philosophy that studies the nature, origin, limits, and validity of human knowledge.

label: phenomenology
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines phenomenology as: Branch of modern philosophy dealing with the description and classification of phenomena.

label: philosophy of art
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines philosophy of art as: The study of the nature of art, including interpretation, representation, expression, and form. It is closely related to "aesthetics," which is the philosophical study of beauty.

label: teleology
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines teleology as: Philosophical study of finality, especially as it pertains to design or purposes in the processes of nature.

label: religion-related disciplines
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religion-related disciplines as: Branches of learning devoted to religion.

label: absolution
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines absolution as: A declaration of forgiveness of sins. In Christianity it refers specifically to the formal remission of sin imparted by a priest or minister either in private after confession or as part of the liturgy in public worship. In Catholicism it is part of the sacrament of penance.

label: afterlife
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines afterlife as: The idea of survival of a person in some form after physical death. This notion is present in a wide variety of forms in different religions.

label: apotheosis
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines apotheosis as: Doctrinal concept concerning the spiritual departure from earthly life or the deification of a person.

label: ascension
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ascension as: The act or process of rising from the earthly to the heavenly sphere. One example is Christ's ascension witnessed by the apostles forty days after his resurrection. Another prime example is the ascent of the Prophet Muhammad to heaven.

label: Buddhist doctrinal concepts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Buddhist doctrinal concepts as: Concepts related to the doctrine of Buddhism.

label: Christian doctrinal concepts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Christian doctrinal concepts as: Concepts related to the doctrine of Christianity.

label: Cihuatlampan
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Cihuatlampan as: Place of women, referring to the western horizon where the Cihuateteoh carry the sun as it sets into Mictlan (the land of the dead).

label: divine light
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines divine light as: Light emanating from a holy personage or visions of supernatural light in general. Usually associated with Christ or the Virgin, and specifically the Transfiguration and the Ascension. For motifs based on the concept of divine light, use "glories."

label: eternity
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines eternity as: Infinite time, which has neither beginning nor end.

label: faith
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines faith as: Act or state of wholeheartedly and steadfastly believing in the existence, power and benevolence of a supreme being.

label: gates of hell
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines gates of hell as: Entrances to the underworld as known in any of various religions and belief systems. The gates of hell may be either apprehended in a material sense to correspond to caves or other places on earth, or conceived of in only an abstract or spiritual sense.

label: heaven
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines heaven as: Place or state of eternal bliss and ideal relationship with God or the gods, usually accorded as the reward for virtue and true religious faith.

label: Hindu doctrinal concepts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Hindu doctrinal concepts as: Concepts related to the doctrine of Hinduism.

label: Jain doctrinal concepts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Jain doctrinal concepts as: Concepts related to the doctrine of Jainism.

label: Mazahuahcan
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Mazahuahcan as: Refers to the conception of the west.

label: Mictlampan
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Mictlampan as: Reference to the North. In the context of Aztec mythology, Mictlampan is associated with Mictlantecuhtli, the god of the dead.

label: purgatory
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines purgatory as: State or place of spiritual cleansing and purification, allowing a purging of sins. A notable example is in the doctrine of the Roman Catholic Church, where it is defined as a state where the souls of those who die in grace undergo such punishment as necessary to expiate their unforgiven venial sins before entering heaven.

label: redemption
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines redemption as: Expiation or atonement for a crime, sin, or offence, including a release from punishment. In theology, deliverance from sin and damnation by atonement or, in Christianity, by the salvation of Christ.

label: reincarnation
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines reincarnation as: The doctrinal concept that some aspect of the self or soul can be reborn any number of times in a new body (animal or human) after death. Fundamental to a number of Eastern religions such as Hinduism and Buddhism, this belief is also found in some modern Western belief systems such as theosophy.

label: salvation
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines salvation as: The doctrinal concept of the deliverance of man or his soul from evil or sin by religious means, the restoration of people to their true state, and the attainment of eternal and blessed life. God's intervention is responsible for salvation in theistic religions while in Buddhism salvation comes from escaping the cycle of birth and rebirth, thereby reaching nirvana.

label: theophany
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines theophany as: The doctrinal concept of divine manifestation, especially the appearance of a god to a human.

label: Tlalocan
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Tlalocan as: In Nahuatl, Tlalocan used as a reference to the East, refers mainly to a place of Tlalocs.

label: Adoptionism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Adoptionism as: Christian doctrine that Jesus of Nazareth became the son of God by exaltation that was not his at birth.

label: agnosticism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines agnosticism as: Doctrine affirming that the existence of God is possible, but denying that there are any sufficient reasons for holding either that God does or does not exist.

label: animism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines animism as: Refers to the belief in spiritual beings capable of influencing human events, based on the idea that animals, plants and even inanimate objects have souls like humans. The 19th-century anthropologist Edward Tylor thought it to be the earliest form of religion, a view not accepted by modern anthropologists.

label: asceticism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines asceticism as: Refers to the practice of self-control and self-denial as an act of religious devotion and a means of achieving greater spiritual awareness; it is found in different forms and to different extents in all religions. Ascetic practices include fasting, a solitary life, meditation, celibacy, the renunciation of possessions, and the mortification of flesh.

label: atheism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines atheism as: Doctrine that there is neither God nor any other deity.

label: Deism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Deism as: Refers most often to the ideas of a heterogeneous religious movement of the late 17th and 18th centuries that flourished mainly in Britain. Deism also became very popular in 18th-century Germany. The movement was concerned with defending the rationality of religion and belief in God in the face of rising skepticism, especially as a consequence of Newton's laws. According to Deist writers, there exists a supreme being who initiated creation and is thus the basis of reality, but who does not intervene in the world and its natural laws (i.e. does not answer prayers or perform miracles). Nevertheless, Deism holds that religion is natural to humanity, and emphasizes natural religion as opposed to revealed religion or the teachings of churches. Natural religion comes from a certain body of religious knowledge that is inborn in everyone or that can be acquired through reason. Important Deist writings include Matthew Tindal's 'Christianity as Old as the Creation' (1730), the so-called 'Deist Bible.' Other important English Deists were Lord Herbert of Cherbury and Anthony Ashley Cooper.

label: Gnosticism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Gnosticism as: Refers to a religious ideology popular in the 4th-century Christian world although it may have had earlier, non-Christian roots stemming from a break from Judaism. The believers in Gnosticism felt that they alone would attain full salvation because they possessed the teachings of Christ regarding the cosmic origins and spiritual destiny of people. It was considered heretic because of its low view of God as Creator, its secret traditions, and its belief that Christ was not really human and that his crucifixion was simply an attempt to fool evil forces.

label: Hasidism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Hasidism as: Refers to a type of Jewish mysticism characterized by an ascetic lifestyle, strict observance of the commandments, and ecstatic forms of worship and prayer. Its origins are usually traced back to Poland in the late 18th century and it was developed in opposition to rabbinic authority and certain Jewish traditions. Hasidism emphasizes prayer as a means of communicating with God as opposed to study of the Torah. As Hasidism spread throughout the world, it was eventually accepted as part of Orthodox Judaism.

label: millenarianism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines millenarianism as: Refers to a Christian religious ideology usually based on an interpretation of Revelation 20. 1-7 which holds that there will be a thousand-year reign of the saints, either right before or after Christ's return. Millenarianism has had its followers since the early days of Christianity, but it became particularly popular in the 19th century, when groups such as the Plymouth Brethren and the Adventists embraced apocalyptic and millennial ideas. Recently the term has also been applied by social scientists to any religious group waiting for a sudden transformation of the world; such groups tend to become popular during times of social change or crisis.

label: monolatry
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines monolatry as: The worship of one god, particularly when it is recognized that other deities exist. In such a system, one god has a central and dominating position, although the principle of polytheism is not abandoned.

label: monotheism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines monotheism as: The religious ideology that there is only one god, as opposed to polytheism and pantheism. Whereas facets of earlier cultures, such as the Egyptians, worshipped one god, a full long-term doctrine of monotheism developed first within Judaism and it remains a central part of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Muslims and Jews think that Christianity's belief in the three aspects of God, the Holy Trinity, denies monotheism.

label: Monothelitism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Monothelitism as: Religious doctrine proposed in 622 and adopted by Byzantine Emperor Heraclius which declared that Jesus Christ had one will but two natures, the divine and the human. This ideology was developed under Patriarch Sergius I of Constantinople in attempt to bridge the gap between Monophysites and Chalcedonians, although neither group accepted it. In 680, the Third Council of Constantinople declared Monothelitism as heretical.

label: paganism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines paganism as: Refers to the religious beliefs and practices of religions outside of the so-called 'major' religions. Pagans are sometimes defined as those who are not Christian, Jewish, or Muslim; occasionally the term is more narrowly used to described any non-Christian, sometimes even Jews.

label: pantheism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pantheism as: Religious ideology based on the belief that God and the universe are ultimately identical, and therefore only the divine is real and sense experience is not. Pantheism is an important element of Hinduism and some schools of Buddhism.

label: Pietism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Pietism as: A religious ideology originally developed within Lutheranism in the 17th and 18th centuries as a reform movement and reaction against rigid Protestant dogmatism. Pietism emphasizes good works, study of the Bible, and devotion. It came to influence other movements and ideologies such as evangelicalism, Methodism, and Moravian Brethren.

label: polytheism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines polytheism as: The religious ideology that there are many gods, as opposed to monotheism. Polytheism is characteristic of primitive religions as well as the religions of ancient Greece and Rome.

label: quietism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines quietism as: Refers generally to the belief that God only works in a person who is completely quiet and passive; religious followers should therefore withdraw from the everyday world and suppress their will. It also refers more specifically to forms of Christian mysticism, particularly to trends in the Middle Ages and 17th-century controversies in Spain and France.

label: shamanism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines shamanism as: Refers generally to the religious practices of some northern Asian peoples who believe that good and evil spirits inhabit the world and can be summoned or heard through inspired priests acting as mediums. Shamanism is also found amongst the pre-Chrisitian Lapps, the Inuit, the Plains Indians of North America, some Australian Aborigines, and some other peoples. The term was originally used by the Tungus people of Siberia.

label: theosophy
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines theosophy as: Any religious or philosophic ideology based on mystical insight into the nature of God or divine truth. This insight is attained only through direct experience of the divine.

label: totemism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines totemism as: Complex of religious and social beliefs and practices whereby individuals or groups of people identify with or consider themselves to be in close kinship or spiritual affinity with a specific natural object or plant or animal species.

label: hagiolatry
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines hagiolatry as: The reverence, worship, or allegiance accorded individuals identified as saints, often expressed through ceremonies, prayers, or other religious rituals.

label: liturgy
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines liturgy as: Refers generally to the prescribed rites of formal and public worship, typically including words, music, symbolic aids, and ritual actions. The diverse forms of liturgy reflect the needs and attitudes of different religious communities. The term can also refer more specifically to the Christian rite of the Eucharist.

label: dian jing
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dian jing as: Used in a garden context, this term refers to accentuating scenic spots. At key scenic points, steps are taken to augment their remarkable appearance. The surrounding structures often are given names related to details of the natural environs, or inscribed with poetry describing the essence of the scenery, thereby contributing details that enhance the aesthetic appeal of the location.

label: empathy
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines empathy as: The capacity for participating in, or a vicarious experiencing of, another's feelings, volitions, or ideas.

label: grandeur
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines grandeur as: The quality of being majestic, magnificent, splendid, stately, or imposing in an awe-inspiring way.

label: Ideal, the
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ideal, the as: The aesthetic quality of the permanent, essential, or eternal character of appearances or other phenomena, which is rooted in an idea of perfection or archetype. It is ultimately derived from from Plato's "Theory of Ideas," which holds that perfection is a concept that is only mirrored imperfectly in real life. This perfection was the ideal to which artists sought to strive in certain periods, styles, or contexts. The concept was particularly evident in various periods of antique art, the Renaissance, and in the 17th- and 18th-century art academies throughout Europe.

label: imperfection
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines imperfection as: The state, quality, or condition of being inaccurate, incomplete, defective and/or displeasing in some way.

label: mimesis
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines mimesis as: Aesthetic concept that takes imitation as the primary operative aspect in the creation of a work.

label: perfection
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines perfection as: The state, quality, or condition of being accurate, complete, without defect and/or delightful.

label: Picturesque, the
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Picturesque, the as: Aesthetic concept or expression, arising in Europe first in painting of the 18th century and later in architecture of the 19th century, characterized by rough, curious, or irregular forms; it applies particularly to rustic landscapes and crumbling buildings having neither the awe-inspiring grandeur of the Sublime nor the order and regularity of beauty.

label: quality
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines quality as: Use in the context of aesthetic judgment for the concept of inherent merit, worthiness, or excellence in something. For the function of selecting quality standards for a project and monitoring the finished work to assure compliance with those standards, use "quality control."

label: sabi
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines sabi as: Aesthetic and poetic ideal particularly important in the Japanese tea ceremony and haiku poetry which advocates taking pleasure and finding tranquility in the old, tarnished and imperfect for their own sake. It is sometimes used synonymously or in conjunction with the concept of "wabi".

label: significant form
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines significant form as: Certain combinations of lines, colors, and spatial elements that excite pure aesthetic emotion; term coined by art critic Clive Bell.

label: Sublime, the
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Sublime, the as: The conception or expression of awe-inspiring grandeur in a work of art.

label: ugliness
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ugliness as: That which evokes an awareness or feeling of deep revulsion or painfully disturbs a previously accepted aesthetic ideal. Can be considered as culturally defined or as an individual reaction.

label: wabi
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines wabi as: An aesthetic ideal advocating for the appreciation of austerity, simplicity, and humility that has deeply influenced Japanese culture. This ideal finds surpassing beauty and deep significance in what is humble or commonplace and appears natural or artless. It expressed in the aesthetic of the tea ceremony, particularly in its ceramics. Its influence can also be seen in the practice of collecting older paintings and works of calligraphy and, more recently, in the rough and natural style of contemporary grass style ink painting. Wabi became a part of a poetic ideal only when it was absorbed into the concept of "sabi".

label: social ethics
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines social ethics as: Ethics that have as their utilitarian end the well-being and fair treatment of the entire community.

label: bad luck
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines bad luck as: A combination of adverse circumstances or events occurring by chance; a person's apparent tendency to have ill fortune; misfortune.

label: good luck
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines good luck as: A combination of favorable circumstances or events occurring by chance; success, prosperity, or advantage apparently brought about by chance rather than through one's own actions or abilities.

label: chaos
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines chaos as: The state of utter confusion and disorder, where everything exists as an undifferentiated, formless mass or mixture. Derived from the original concept in ancient Greek cosmology, meaning the primevil emptiness of the universe before distinct entities came into being.

label: dialectic
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dialectic as: Originally in ancient Greece, a form of logical argumentation proceeding by question and answer. In modern times it is the idea that internal contradictions are transcended, but then give rise to new contradictions that themselves must be resolved. As a concept of evolution, it applies to diverse fields including philosophy, nature, and history.

label: identity
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines identity as: Those characteristics or conditions of a thing, person, or group that remain the same amid change or that distinguish a thing, person, or group from another.

label: presence
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines presence as: Concept regarding the condition of being present in front of, or in the same place with a person or thing.

label: supernatural
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines supernatural as: Beyond or outside of the natural order. The term is typically used to refer to events or phenomena that are not explicable given the existing characterizations of nature. Occult phenomena and extrasensory perception are examples.

label: absurdism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines absurdism as: A philosophical movement or attitude associated with Albert Camus that posits that humanity's search for meaning is futile in a chaotic, senseless universe.

label: anthropomorphism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines anthropomorphism as: Interpretation of what is not human in terms of human characteristics.

label: Aristotelianism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Aristotelianism as: Philosophy incorporating essential features of the thinking of Aristotle.

label: Augustinianism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Augustinianism as: Refers to the philosophical and theological ideas and doctrines derived from the work of Augustine (354-430), bishop of Hippo, and associated with the Augustinian orders. The intellectual tradition of Augustinianism has been influential since the Middle Ages, when it developed. Augustine offered an optimistic ontology and an escape from skepticism. He also formulated a cosmic theory to account for the plurality of form in the world and to reconcile it with the uniqueness of God's creative act. Augustine also described the ultimate goal of human life as a life of beatitude combined with ethical-political concern. Primacy of faith, knowledge of the soul, divine illumination, and grace are all essential aspects of Augustinianism. Augustine believed that truth resided in man's soul and it was this truth alone that instructs man. This truth, the greatest proof of God's existence, confers joy and happiness. Augustine's speculation on the Trinity and predestination were also highly influential.

label: determinism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines determinism as: Doctrine that all acts of will result from causes which determine them either in such a manner that people have no alternative course of action, or that the will is still free in the sense of being uncompelled. Determinism holds that all behaviors and events are determined by God or by the laws of the universe before they occur. Determinism takes different forms in religions, but the basic issue is how to reconcile the omnipotence of God or the inevitable effects of karma with the freedom and resposibility of a individual person.

label: dualism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dualism as: Doctrine that the universe is under the dominion of two opposing principles, one of which is good and the other evil.

label: globalism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines globalism as: The approach to social, cultural, scientific, ecological, or humanistic questions involving an orientation to the world as a single interacting system, and the placing of its interests above those of individual regions or nations. For the similar theory or belief discussed or applied specifically in the context of politics and political science, use "internationalism."

label: holism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines holism as: Theory according to which a whole cannot be analyzed without residue into the sum of its parts or reduced to discrete elements.

label: individualism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines individualism as: The ethical doctrine or principle that the interests of the individual are or ought to be paramount in determination of conduct.

label: nihilism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines nihilism as: Extreme form of skepticism that denies the objective reality of all values, beliefs, and truths.

label: nominalism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines nominalism as: Theory that there are no universal essences in reality, that the mind can frame no single concept or image corresponding to any universal or general term, and that only individual concrete entities have existence.

label: Platonism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Platonism as: Refers to the philosophy of Plato or to any philosophy inspired by Plato, especially to Plato's idea that the phenomena perceived by the senses are an imperfect and transitory reflection of the ideal forms of an unchanging and eternal reality. This absolute reality (or realities) gives value and meaning to everything's existence, particularly to human life.

label: pluralism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pluralism as: Philosophical theory that recognizes more than one ultimate reality or value, each capable of rational support and all appropriately included as options for individual choice. For the cultural movement promoting the full participation of diverse ethnic, racial, religious, or social groups within the larger community, use "multiculturalism."

label: positivism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines positivism as: The philosophical doctrine of Auguste Comte and his successors. It asserts that knowledge of reality can be achieved only through the particular sciences and ordinary observation.

label: pragmatism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pragmatism as: Philosophical movement, dominant in the United States during the first quarter of the 20th century, based on the principle that the usefulness, workability, and practicality of ideas, policies, and proposals are the criteria of their merit. It stresses the priority of action over doctrine, of experience over fixed principles, and it holds that ideas borrow their meanings from their consequences and their truths from their verification.

label: rasquachismo
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines rasquachismo as: Perspective, or sensibility of the underdog, or the view of the downtrodden. The term is used specifically within the Chicano and Chicano artist community, specifically for purposes of defining identity.

label: scholasticism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines scholasticism as: The philosophical systems and speculative tendencies of various Medieval Christian thinkers, who, working against a background of fixed religious dogma, sought to solve anew general philosophical problems (as of faith and reason, will and intellect, and the provability of the existence of God), initially under the influence of the mystical and intuitional tradition of patristic philosophy, and especially Augustinianism, and later under that of Aristotle.

label: stoicism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines stoicism as: A philosophical movement that flourished in Greek and Roman antiquity. Stoics have always believed that the goal of all inquiry is to provide humanity with a mode of conduct characterized by tranquility of mind and certainty of moral worth, and urged participation in the affairs of humankind. Thus, moral worth, duty, and justice are singularly Stoic emphases, together with a certain sternness of mind.

label: syncretism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines syncretism as: Reconciliation or union of conflicting (as religious) beliefs or an effort intending such.

label: transcendentalism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines transcendentalism as: A philosophic movement based on an idealistic belief in the essential unity of all things, the innate goodness of man, and the supremacy of insight over logic and experience in understanding reality and ascertaining truths. It is considered to be a part of the Romantic movement and had a powerful impact on the arts, particularly literature. The term generally refers to 19th-century transcendentalism in New England although the movement was found in other countries including Germany and England.

label: utilitarianism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines utilitarianism as: Doctrine that usefulness is the highest good and that the determining characteristic of right conduct should be the usefulness of its consequence.

label: choreography
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines choreography as: The aspect of the discipline of dance that involves inventing or arranging and putting together steps, gestures, and patterns to form dances, and separate dances to form a dance composition.

label: music theory
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines music theory as: Discipline involving the study of the theoretical aspects of music and its notation, typically as opposed to actual performance.

label: vocal arts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines vocal arts as: Discipline involving the study of singing and other vocal expressions, including performance.

label: dramaturgy
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dramaturgy as: Describes the discipline of theatrical or dramatic composition, representation, and research. English dramaturgy is derived from German Dramaturgie, a concept developed by the German dramatist and critic Gotthold Lessing in a series of essays entitled 'Hamburgische Dramaturgie,' published 1767 to 1769. The discipline includes researching, selection, adaptation, or development of texts, scripts, plays, operas, or films for a theater or other production company.

label: computer music
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines computer music as: Musical works not in a specific form or of a specific type in which sound is generated or composed solely by computers or other electronic data-processing machinery via software or other means.

label: granular synthesis
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines granular synthesis as: A method for generating sound involving the combination of tiny waveform fragments to create larger acoustic events. This is generally achieved with the use of digital computers.

label: musique concrète
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines musique concrète as: Musical works created by recording natural sounds and subsequently altering and rearranging them into a composition. The word "concrète" refers to the method of working directly with sound rather than a system of abstract musical notation. Originally recorded onto discs, these works were later realized with magnetic tape as the technology became available. Developed by the French composer Pierre Schaeffer and colleagues, including Pierre Henry, in the Club d'Essai and Groupe de Recherches Musicales at the Office de Radio-diffusion et Télévision Française ca. 1948. The term "musique concrète" is reserved for works created solely with naturally occurring sounds recorded onto disc or magnetic tape. For works created from sounds generated primarily by electronic synthesis, or using combinations of natural and synthesized sound, use "electronic music."

label: Noh
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Noh as: Important form of classical Japanese dance drama that has been performed since the 14th century. It is often based on stories from traditional literature with a supernatural being transformed into human form as a hero telling a story. Noh integrates masks, costumes and various props into a dance-based performance, Emotions are mainly conveyed through stylized conventional gestures.

label: twelve-tone music
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines twelve-tone music as: A body of musical compositions created since the early part of the 20th century created using the twelve-tone system attributed to Arnold Schoenberg. Generally twelve-tone music is considered a subset of serial music, but there is some disagreement on this.

label: architectural criticism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines architectural criticism as: The study or practice of the analytical description, interpretation, and evaluation of architectural works.

label: architectural history
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines architectural history as: Study of the development over time of the human built environment.

label: art criticism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines art criticism as: The study or practice of the analytical description, interpretation, and evaluation of visual art works and exhibitions.

label: art history
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines art history as: Study of the visual arts within a historical framework, from from prehistory to the present, including stylistic development, use of art in communication and decoration, and the aesthetic and intellectual value of art. It first became a dedicated field of study in the 19th century Western world.

label: art therapy
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines art therapy as: Study and practice of the therapeutic use of images and objects, to foster nonverbal communication, creativity, and physical interaction, and to uncover verbal associations and interpretations, helping to identify and understand patients' emotional, motor, and perceptual dysfunctions.

label: musicology
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines musicology as: Scientific and orderly investigation and study of music and related areas, including history, theory, music education, acoustics, psychology, and social and cultural aspects.

label: applied linguistics
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines applied linguistics as: Branch of linguistics where the primary concern is the application of linguistic theories, methods, and findings to practical language problems, such as language teaching, lexicography, translation, stylistics, and speech therapy.

label: theoretical linguistics
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines theoretical linguistics as: Branch of linguistics where the primary aim is to establish universal principles for the study of language and languages, and to determine the underlying structure and other characteristics of human language.

label: cryptography
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines cryptography as: The practice of writing in code or symbols.

label: cryptology
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines cryptology as: The discipline concerned with data communication and storage in secure and usually secret form, including the science, study, or practice of encrypting and decrypting information.

label: etymology
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines etymology as: Study of the history of a particular word or element of a word, or of historical linguistic change.

label: semiotics
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines semiotics as: Theory and study of signs and symbols dealing especially with their function in languages, including syntax, semantics, and pragmatics.

label: process philosophy
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines process philosophy as: Refers to the theistic philosophy that views creative becoming as the universal form of reality and emphasizes the relational nature of all being.

label: anthropology of religion
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines anthropology of religion as: Study of religion using the methods and theories of anthropology.

label: comparative religion
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines comparative religion as: Comparative study of the characteristics of religious systems in different societies that focuses on the origin and evolution of religious beliefs and practices from earlier or less urbanized societies to modern ones, aims to develop a universal evolutionary continuum of religions, and stresses a scientific methodology. For the comparative study of religions that largely disregards evolutionary schemes and features a primarily historical methodology, use "religious history."

label: philosophy of religion
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines philosophy of religion as: The philosophical study of religion, especially concerning the rationality of religious beliefs, and the descriptive analysis and elucidation of religious language, belief, and practice.

label: psychology of religion
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines psychology of religion as: Branch of religious study in which religious thought, experience, and behavior are studied using the concepts and methodology of psychology.

label: sociology of religion
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines sociology of religion as: Study of religion using the sociological method of approach.

label: biblical studies
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines biblical studies as: Critical study of the Bible and biblical writings, including such approaches as textual analysis, historical study, exegesis, hermeneutics, and literary and linguistic criticism.

label: church history
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines church history as: Study of the history of the Christian Church and its sects and branches.

label: ecclesiology
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ecclesiology as: Study of the doctrines of the church, including the study of ecclesiastical art, antiquities, and the adornment and equipment of churches.

label: eschatology
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines eschatology as: The science or teachings concerned with last things, such as the end of history or of the present world, the fate of the soul after death, the final judgment of individuals, and the creation or restoration of a perfect world.

label: religious ethics
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religious ethics as: Study of ethics inspired and informed by religious doctrine, faith, and experience, also the study of religious doctrine and commitment with reference to ethics.

label: religious history
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religious history as: Refers to the comparative historical study of the nature and structure of the world's religions and their diverse manifestations over time in different societies and cultures. For the comparative study of the characteristics of religious systems in different societies that aims to develop a universal evolutionary continuum of religions and stresses a scientific methodology, see "comparative religion."

label: arhats
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines arhats as: Buddhist saints, the most accomplished of the four types of who have defeated all afflictions and will enter nirvana upon death. Typically depicted as 16 in number, who vowed to remain alive to preserve his teachings.

label: bardo
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines bardo as: In Tibetan Buddhism, the intermediate state between death and rebirth. Bardo, which can last up to 49 days, follows a vision of a beam of clear light by the dying person.

label: bhūmi
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines bhūmi as: The earth, floor, or foundation, symbolically stages of enlightenment in Buddhist practice.

label: buddha field
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines buddha field as: In Buddhism, realms of individual bodhisattvas who have attained awakening; may have varying spiritual climates or degrees of perfection, either pure or mixed.

label: dharma
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dharma as: Refers to a key concept with multiple meanings in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism. In Hinduism, dharma is the religious and moral law governing and enabling society and individual conduct. It is found in the early religious manuals called the dharmasutras and has been expanded into larger compilations of law called the dharmashastra. Dharma in Buddhism retains the Hindu sense of cosmic law and order but it also came to be applied to the teachings of the Buddha who is seen as a manifestation of the universal truth that is dharma. Thus, dharma is the practice of this truth in Buddhism. The triratna ("three jewels") is a fundamental aspect of Buddhism and consists of the Buddha, dharma, and the sangha (community of believers). In the context of Buddhist metaphysics, the term in the plural (dharmas) refers to the interrelated elements that make up the empirical world. In addition to being commonly understood as moral virtue in Jaina philosophy, dharma also refers to an eternal "substance" (dravya) that is the medium that allows living beings to move. It is a meaning unique to Jainism. The term may simply refer to the teachings of the Jinas. For the Jains, dharma has its opposite in adharma which is error and immorality as well as the ability to rest or pause.

label: dhyana
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dhyana as: In Hinduism and Buddhism, a type of profound meditation; the penultimate (seventh) stage of yoga.

label: karma
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines karma as: The chain of causation that drives all phenomena, in which virtuous actions lead to future happiness and evil acts the opposite. The sum of a person's actions in one of his successive states of existence, regarded as determining his fate in the next. Among symbols for karma is the endless knot. Karma is a key concept in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism, and Taoism.

label: mappō
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines mappō as: The clearest expression of apocalyptic thought in Japanese Buddhism, this third and final age of Buddhism was believed to have begun in 1052. During this end of the Buddhist Law, Buddhism is thought to degenerate to the point where the teaching still exists, but there is no true practice of it. This religious pessimism and preparation for the end times caused a flurry of art commissions during the late Heian period in areas such as sculpture, calligraphy, painting and temple building by wealthy aristocrats who hoped to gain salvation by honoring Amida Buddha.

label: nirvana
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines nirvana as: Concept of state of deep inner freedom and peace, the supreme goal of Hinduism and Buddhism. Reaching nirvana means liberation from samsara, the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. In Buddhism, nirvana represents freedom from attachments and individual consciousness and the attainment of tranquility and purity. Nirvana is conceived somewhat differently within the various schools of Buddhism. In Hinduism it furthermore means that union with God or the Absolute is possible.

label: pure land
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pure land as: In Mahayana Buddhism, pure abodes or celestial realms of a buddha or bodhisattva; used for East Asian Buddhism, Taoism, and Bon. For realms both pure and mixed, use "buddha fields."

label: satori
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines satori as: In Zen Buddhism, satori refers to a sudden personal enlightenment analagous to the original moment of spiritual rebirth experienced by the Gautama Buddha.

label: uṣṇīsạ
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines uṣṇīsạ as: Physical mark identifying a buddha, conventionally depicted as a cranial bump and said to possess magical properties.

label: consubstantiation
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines consubstantiation as: The doctrine according to which the substances of both the body and blood of Christ and of the bread and wine coexist in the eucharistic elements after being consecrated. The concept is attributed to Luther, who was opposed to the doctrine of transubstantiation. Luther illustrated the concept with the analogy of an iron in a fire: the fire and the iron are united in the red-hot iron yet both are still present.

label: immaculate conception
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines immaculate conception as: The Christian doctrinal concept that the Virgin Mary was free from original sin from the moment of conception, unlike all other humans after Adam and Eve. Although this belief was promulgated as Roman Catholic dogma by Pope Pius IX in 1854, it has been rejected by Protestants and the Orthodox Church.

label: stigmatization
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines stigmatization as: The appearance of wounds on the hands, feet, and side corresponding to those received by Christ upon crucifixion, which have appeared, inexplicably, on some people who intensely contemplate the Passion of Christ.

label: avatara
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines avatara as: Refers to the descent to earth of a Hindu deity in a visible form. The word comes from the Sanskrit meaning 'descent.' The concept comes from the tradition associated with the deity Vishnu who periodically appeared on earth in human or animal form in order to save it from severe danger or destruction. Vishnu's most famous manifestations have been as Krishna and Rama. The deity is expected to return in the last of his forms to destroy and subsequently recreate the world at a time when it is completely depraved. In more recent times the concept has been challenged by reformers, particularly in regards to manifestations in animal forms. At the same time, others have put forward the idea that humans, even non-Hindus such as Jesus or Muhammad, can become avataras by a divine infilling.

label: bhakti
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines bhakti as: In Hinduism, loving and adoring devotion to God or to one's chosen manifestation of the divine that leads to a close personal relationship with God. By surrendering to God, one can receive grace, however low one's station. In most religious texts of popular Hinduism, bhakti is recommended as the most effective path to the divine. This concept is behind some of the world's most moving theistic poetry.

label: moksha
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines moksha as: In Hinduism, liberation from samsara, the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. This liberation would mean a state of bliss (ananda), freedom from sorrow and higher awareness. It is the fourth and ultimate artha (goal) for Hindus, attained when ignorance, desire, and all attachments are overcome. There are various interpretations of moksha, especially in regard to how it is attained, whether by personal effort, by grace of a personal god, or a combination of the two. In Jainism, moksha lies beyond enlightenment and is freedom from the impediment of karma; enlightenment provides the means for rooting out all remaining karma.

label: pañcadēvōpāsanā
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pañcadēvōpāsanā as: Worship of five divinities: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, Gaṇapati, and Śakti.

label: samsara
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines samsara as: The cycle of death and rebirth experienced by all unawakened beingsover potentially infinite eons consisting often of six destinies: (1) divinity, (2) demigod, (3) human, (4) animal, (5) ghost, and (6) hell dweller in Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism. Although debated, the concept is probably of non-Vedic or heterodox origin.

label: trimurti
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines trimurti as: Hindu concept of the collapse of the three main Hindu gods, Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva, into a single form with three faces. Some scholars consider the trimurti as a way to reconcile different monotheistic approaches with one another and with the concept of ultimate reality (Brahman) since the trimurti manifests the cosmic functions of the Supreme Being. The trimurti was classically expressed in the poem 'Kumarasambhava' by Kalidasa (ca. 4th-5th century).

label: ahimsa
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ahimsa as: Refers to the principle of respect for all life and the practice of non-injury to all living beings; it is found in Buddhism, some Hindu sects, and especially Jainism. Ahimsa is based on the belief that all living creatures are sacred and that violence has negative effects on those who commit it, for example, harming a living thing may result in an unfavorable reincarnation. The term comes from the Sanskrit meaning 'not-harming.'

label: cāraṇa
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines cāraṇa as: In Jainism, cāraṇa refers to the 'capability to move in the sky,' one of the eight extraordinary powers of mythical flying ascetics.

label: image quality
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines image quality as: Use with reference to photographic and electronic images, usually pertaining to the clarity of details, often relating to the degree of resolution.

label: group identity
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines group identity as: An individual person's conscious sharing of some kind of essential character with one or more groups of other people, such as a race, nation, social class, profession, or body of people organized into a group at some particular time for some particular purpose.

label: Neo-Platonism
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Neo-Platonism as: Refers to a philosophy developed by Plotinus in Alexandria in the 3rd century CE that consists of a modified version of Platonism combined with aspects of Judaic and Christian thought and possibly Oriental mysticism. Neo-Platonism holds that there is one source from which all existence comes from and with which an individual soul can be mystically united; it also emphasizes the plurality of levels of being, with the physical universe perceptible to the senses being the lowest. Neo-Platonism developed in a variety of forms over many centuries and it has enjoyed numerous revivals and modifications throughout history.

label: amalgam style
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines amalgam style as: Style that combines recognizable elements of two or more defined styles.

label: ancient
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ancient as: In the discipline of art and architectural history, typically refers to the period in Europe, Asia Minor, and north Africa, prior to the fall of the western Roman Empire. The term is also sometimes applied more generally to prehistory and to early cultures in other areas of the world.

label: Archaeological Style
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Archaeological Style as: Style of visual arts that intentionally imitates ancient objects or style. Most often used to refer to jewelry design, but may also be applied to paintings, sculpture, and occasionally to architecture.

label: geologic time scale
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines geologic time scale as: An internationally recognized time scale of Earth's history since the planet's formative period subdivided into eons, eras, periods, and epochs.

label: Late Glacial
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Late Glacial as: Designating the latter part of the last Quaternary glacial period, immediately preceding the current postglacial period, marked predominantly by the retreat of glaciers.

label: Post-Colonial
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Post-Colonial as: Basic reference to 'after the colonial" condition, periods, and cultures of peoples, states, and societies that have been through a process of formal decolonization. Since the 1980s the term is used to also refer to the trend to question Western knowledge, categories, and assumptions.

label: prehistoric
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines prehistoric as: Refers to the period antecedent to the first contemporary written accounts of a people. The time span for this period varies according to specific local habitation patterns and in different scholarly disciplines.

label: protohistoric
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines protohistoric as: Periods and cultures between prehistory and history, during which a culture or civilization has not yet developed writing, but other cultures have provided written historical records for this people in a given area.

label: three-age system
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines three-age system as: Division of human prehistory into three ages: the Stone Age, the Bronze Age, and the Iron Age.

label: Antarctic
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Antarctic as: Having to do with the style or culture of the south polar region of the earth, which comprises the continent of Antarctica together with the seas and islands of the Southern Ocean. Also refers to the flora, fauna, geography, oceanography, or climate of the region.

label: Asian
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Asian as: Refers to the cultures of the continent of Asia, which is in the eastern hemisphere, and is bounded by the Pacific Ocean, the Indian Ocean, the Arctic Ocean, and is generally considered to be delimited on the west by the Ural Mountains. It also refers to the numerous islands off the coast of Asia.

label: Early Western World
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Early Western World as: Refers to a style region encompassing the Mediterranean and the Occident.

label: European
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines European as: Styles, periods, and cultures of the continent of Europe, which is in the northern hemisphere, is bounded by the Arctic Ocean, the Atlantic Ocean, and the Mediterranean Sea, and is generally considered to be delimited on the east by the Ural Mountains.

label: Global
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Global as: Styles, periods, and cultures that cross boundaries of multiple nations and regions.

label: Islamic World, The
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Islamic World, The as: Refers to a style region encompassing the regions where Islam is prevalent.

label: Middle Eastern
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Middle Eastern as: Styles and cultures existing in the extensive area that includes the nations of southwest Asia and northeastern Africa. The term was formerly used to also include Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, and Burma.

label: Oceanic
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Oceanic as: Cultures and styles of various regions in Oceania, comprising islands scattered throughout the Pacific Ocean (generally excluding Japan, Indonesia, and the Philippines), but including Australia.

label: The Americas
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines The Americas as: Refers to a style region encompassing North, Central and South America.

label: bungalow style
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines bungalow style as: Style of domestic architecture with a one- to one-and-a-half-story building having a low-pitched gable or hipped roof, with widely projecting, often bracketed eaves, dormers, and conspicuous front porches.

label: military style
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines military style as: Style of fashion, decorative arts, and architecture that invoke elements of miliary design and architecture.

label: old-fashioned
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines old-fashioned as: A style that belongs to or resembles a style or fashion of an earlier time. The term refers not to an absolute time frame, but is relative to the period being discussed, not to the present. For example, a style popular in 1710 may in 2010 be said to have been "old fashioned" in 1750. "Old fashioned" differs from "retro" in implying that a style or object is antiquated, outdated, and sometimes unfashionable in form or character, while "retro" implies reference to a previous style (usually from the mid-20th century) that is still considered desirable and popular for its nostalgic value.

label: period style
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines period style as: Term referring to any generic style, particularly in the context of interior design, characterized by the incorporation of antiques or replicas of antiques of one particular named style, usually styles from 18th and 19th-century Europe and the United States (e.g., American Colonial, Louis XIV, Hepplewhite, etc.).

label: plantation house style
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines plantation house style as: Style of architecture, interior design, or other works that evokes elements of plantation houses of the American south or of Hawaii or other island colonial settlements. Particulary appropriate when the work is not affiliated with a plantation, but only the style is appropriated.

label: pre-colonial
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pre-colonial as: General term designating a culture, style, or period occurring or existing before the colonial period of a country. Often used in reference to indigenous cultures prior to European colonization.

label: ranch style
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ranch style as: Style of domestic architecture, particularly in North American 1940s-1950s. Characterized by having one-story and low-pitched roofs.

label: shabby chic
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines shabby chic as: A style, particularly in the context of interior design, characterized by European or American antiques or replicas of antiques that that show evidence of wear and age, such as layers of paint that are worn and chipped and faded or muted fabrics. The style first developed in Britain. The term was coined in the "World of Interiors" magazine in the 1980s and has become a registered trademark for a US company.

label: plastic arts
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines plastic arts as: In general, refers to the visual arts as opposed to literature, poetry, or other writing. In a narrower sense, it sometimes refers to all visual arts concerned with three-dimensional objects, but not two-dimensional visual arts. For works made of the material plastic, use "plastic (organic material)."

label: technical art history
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines technical art history as: Refers to an emerging interdisciplinary field which seeks to integrate scientific study of art into the practice of art history; and the interpretative methods of the art historian into the conservation lab. An outgrowth of the subdiscipline of art history once known as Technical Studies, the field has recently established itself within graduate program curricula.

label: automotive design
summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines automotive design as: Practice and discipline of designing the appearance, ergonomics, complex systems, and other aspects of motor vehicles, usually road vehicles such as automobiles, motorcycles, trucks, buses, coaches, and vans.

label: communication design
